title: Commentariorum In Epistolam Beati Pauli Ad Philemonem Liber Unus
author: Jerome
source: Translated by Claude from tmp486.tmp486.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: 741-742 Qui nolunt inter Epistolas P(??)uli eam re- cipere quae ad Philemonem scribitur, aiunt, non sem- per a Apostolum, necomnia, Christo in se loquente, di- xisse : quia nec humana imbecillitas unum tenorem sancti Spiritus ferre potuisset : nec hujus corpusculi necessitates [Al, necessitas] sub praesentia Domini semper complerentur : velut disponere prandium, cibum capere, esurire, saturari, ingesta digerere, exhausta complere;
passages.english: Those who refuse to accept among the Letters of Paul the one written to Philemon say that the Apostle did not always speak, nor speak everything, with Christ speaking in him: because human weakness could not have borne a single unbroken course of the Holy Spirit, nor would the necessities of this poor little body be always fulfilled in the presence of the Lord: such as arranging a meal, taking food, being hungry, being filled, digesting what has been taken in, replenishing what has been spent;
passages.notes: "741-742" is a column number from the printed edition and is not translated. The stray "a" before "Apostolum" is a footnote mark and is left out. "P(??)uli" is read as "Pauli".

passages.original: Siquidem et ille Saul, rex Judaeae, persecutor David, de tribu Benjamin fuit. Quod autem Saulus a nobis dicitur, non mirum est Hebraea nomina ad similitu- dinem Graecorum et Romanorum casuum declinari, ut sicut pro Joseph, Josephus : pro Jacob, Jacobus : ita pro Saul quoque, Saulus in nostra lingua ac ser- mone dicatur. Quaeritur igitur, cur, aut quo jubente, vel antiquum nomen amiserit, vel novum sumpserit. Ut ex Abram, Abraham diceretur, Dei jussione per- fectum est (Gen.
passages.english: For indeed that Saul too, king of Judaea, the persecutor of David, was of the tribe of Benjamin. But as for his being called Saulus by us, it is no wonder that Hebrew names are declined after the likeness of Greek and Roman cases, so that just as for Joseph [we say] Josephus, and for Jacob, Jacobus, so also for Saul, Saulus is said in our language and speech. The question, then, is why, or at whose command, he either lost his old name or took up a new one. That Abram should be called Abraham was accomplished by the command of God (Gen.
passages.notes: The passage ends mid-reference; the citation continues in the following text (Gen. xvii). Scanning breaks such as 'similitu- dinem', 'ser- mone' and 'per- fectum' have been read as single words.

passages.original: Non omnis autem qui vinctus est vinctus est Christi; sed quicumque pro Christi nomine et pro ejus confessione vincitur, ille vere vinctus dicitur Jesu Christi, et sanguis effusus is tantum martyrem facit, qui pro Christi nomine fun- ditur. Scribit igitur ad Philemonem Romae vinctus in carcerc, quo tempore mihi videntur ad Philippen- ses, Colossenses, et Ephesios Epistolae esse dictatae. Ad Philippenses illa ex causa : primum quod cum solo Timotheo scribit, quod et in hac Epistola fa- cit.
passages.english: Not everyone who is in chains, however, is a prisoner of Christ; but whoever is chained for the name of Christ and for confessing him is truly called a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and shed blood makes a martyr only when it is poured out for the name of Christ. So he writes to Philemon while in chains in prison at Rome, at which time, it seems to me, the Letters to the Philippians, Colossians, and Ephesians were dictated. [I say so of the Letter] to the Philippians for this reason: first, because he writes together with Timothy alone, which he also does in this Letter.

passages.original: Et hoc circumcisio de populo Judaico accipiendum putans, impegit in lapidem of- fensionis, et petram scandali : non recogitans vineam quae de AEgypto translata est, esse domum Israel, et Christum hic dici vel diligibilem, vel dilectum : dum et ipse diligi meretur a sanctis, et sancti eum dili- gunt, offerentes ei magis charitatem, quam ulla [Al. alia] charitatis praemia postulantes. Scribunt igitur Paulus et Thimotheus, Philemoni charissimo et cooperatori : qui ideo charissimus dictus est, quod in eodem Christi opere versetur. Apphiae [Al. Appiae] quoque sorori, non habenti in se falsae ali- quid, et fictae germanitatis : et Archippo commili- toni, quem arbitror cum Paulo et Thimotheo contra adversarios pro Christi nomine dimicantem exstitisse victorem, et propterea nunc commilitonem dici, quod in codem certamine belloque superaverit.
passages.english: And the circumcision, thinking this was to be understood of the Jewish people, struck against the stone of stumbling and the rock of offence: not reflecting that the vine brought over from Egypt is the house of Israel, and that Christ is here called either 'lovable' or 'beloved', since he both deserves to be loved by the saints and the saints love him, offering him love rather than demanding any rewards for love. So Paul and Timothy write to Philemon, dearest and fellow worker, who is called dearest because he is engaged in the same work of Christ. [They write] also to Apphia the sister, who had in herself nothing false or feigned in [her] sisterhood; and to Archippus the fellow soldier, who, I think, fighting with Paul and Timothy against adversaries for the name of Christ, came out the victor, and is therefore now called fellow soldier, because he prevailed in the same contest and war.
passages.notes: The opening sentence is elliptical; "circumcisio" (the circumcision, i.e. Jewish interpreters) appears to be the subject of "impegit", though the syntax is awkward and may be corrupt. "Al." readings are alternative manuscript readings given by the edition.

passages.original: nunc autem et tibi, et mihi utilis est : quem remisi tibi. Tu autem illum, id est mea viscera, suscipe, quem ego volueram mecum detinere, ut pro te mihi ministraret in vinculis Evangelii. Volens impe- trare quod postulat, jam non pro servo Philemonis, sed pro filio suo se asserit deprecari; et de illo fi- lio quem genuerit in vinculis Evangelii, hoc est, quae pro Christi Evangelio sustinebat : qui cum ante inutilis domino suo tantum fuerit (necenim servus fur atque fugitivus alteri nocuit, nisi domino suo) nunc econtrario utilitatis compensatione, qua ipsi domino et Paulo utilis est, caeterisque per Paulum, plus charitatis meretur, quam odii ante meruerat.
passages.english: "but now he is useful both to you and to me: I have sent him back to you. Receive him, that is, my own heart, whom I had wanted to keep with me, so that he might serve me on your behalf in the chains of the Gospel." Wishing to obtain what he asks, he declares that he is pleading no longer for Philemon's slave but for his own son, and for that son whom he begot in the chains of the Gospel, that is, the chains he was bearing for the Gospel of Christ. Though before he had been useless only to his master (for a slave who is a thief and a runaway harmed no one but his master), now on the contrary, by the compensation of usefulness, by which he is useful to his master himself and to Paul, and to the rest through Paul, he deserves more love than he had previously deserved hatred.

passages.original: Apostolus non fruitur nisi eo qui multas in se habet concinen- tesque virtutes, et totum quod b Christus dicitur pro varietate causarum : sapientiam videlicet, ju- stitiam, continentiam, mansuetudinem, temperan- tiam, castitatem : has imprecatur Philemoni : ut cum his abundaverit, ipse eo perfruens impleatur. Et ne putes illam fruitionem dici, qua nos saepe no- stri inter nos praesentia delectamur, addidit, in Do- mino : ut ex eo quod Domini nomen adjunctum est, intelligeretur, et alia esse fruitio, qua quis absque Domino perfruatur.
passages.english: The Apostle does not 'enjoy' anyone except one who has in himself many harmonious virtues, and the whole of what Christ is called according to the variety of circumstances: namely wisdom, justice, continence, gentleness, temperance, chastity. These he prays for Philemon, so that when he abounds in them, [Paul] himself, enjoying him, may be filled. And lest you think that enjoyment is meant by which we often delight in one another's presence, he added 'in the Lord', so that from the addition of the Lord's name it might be understood that there is also another enjoyment, which someone may enjoy apart from the Lord.
passages.notes: The stray "b" before "Christus" is a footnote mark and is left out. The clause about 'another enjoyment … apart from the Lord' is so in the text; the sense is that the enjoyment meant here is distinguished from that other kind.

passages.original: Refice viscera mea in Christo. Sicut ipse frui vult Philemone in Domino : ita viscera sua Onesimum, quem et superius eodem nomine appellavit, refici vult per Philemonem, et ambigue dictum : utrum viscera Pauli in Christo Onesimus sit : an viscera Pauli Onesimus per Philemonem in Christo refi- cienda sint.
passages.english: "Refresh my heart in Christ." Just as he himself wishes to enjoy Philemon in the Lord, so he wishes his own heart, Onesimus, whom he also called by the same name above, to be refreshed by Philemon. And it is said ambiguously: whether Onesimus is Paul's heart in Christ, or whether Onesimus, Paul's heart, is to be refreshed in Christ by Philemon.

passages.original: Hoc si se ita habeat, et Aristarchus qui con- captivus ejus in a eadem Epistola dicitur, ad eam- dem intelligentiam deducetur : nisi forte reconditum aliquid, et sacratum, ut quidam putant, in verbo captivitatis ostenditur [Al. ostendit], quod capti pa- ri er et vincti, in vallem hanc adducti [Al. deduct] sint lacrymarum. Quod si neutrum recipitur, ex eo quod hic additum est in Christo Jesu, possumus su- spicari eadem eum Romae pro Christo vincula susti- nuisse quae Paulum : et ut vinctum Christi, ita ca- ptivum quoque ejus potuisse dici. Aut certe ita, quod nobilis et ipse sit in apostolis, ut Andronicus et Ju- lia, de quibus ad Romanos scribitur : Salutate An- dronicum, et Juliam cognatos, et concaptivos meos, qui sunt nobiles in apostolis, qui et ante me fuerunt in Christo Jesu (Rom. xvi, 7). Haec de Epaphra. Caete- rum cooperatores Evangelii et vinculorum suorum, cum ad Philemonem epistolam scriberet, Marcum ponit, quem puto Evangelii conditorem, et Aristar- chum cujus supra fecimus mentionem, et Demam, de quo in alio loco queritur : Demas me dereliquit, diligens praesens saeculum, et abiit Thessalonicam. Et Lucam medicum, qui Evangelium et Actus Aposto- lorum Ecclesiis derelinquens, quomodo Apostoli de piscatoribus piscium, piscatores hominum facti sunt (Matth. iv) : ita de medico corporum, in medicum est versus animarum, de quo et in alio loco : Misi, inquit, cum illo fratrem, cujus laus est in Evangelio per omnes Ecclesias (Il Cor. viii, 18) : cujus liber quotiescumque legitur in Ecclesiis, toties ejus me- dicina non cessat.
passages.english: If this is so, Aristarchus too, who is called his fellow captive in the same Letter, will be brought to the same understanding: unless perhaps something hidden and sacred, as some think, is shown in the word 'captivity', namely that they were taken captive and chained alike and brought into this valley of tears. But if neither is accepted, from the fact that 'in Christ Jesus' is added here, we can suppose that he bore at Rome for Christ the same chains as Paul, and that, as he could be called a prisoner of Christ, so he could also be called his captive. Or certainly thus: that he too is notable among the apostles, like Andronicus and Julia, of whom it is written to the Romans: "Greet Andronicus and Julia, my kinsmen and fellow captives, who are notable among the apostles, who were also in Christ Jesus before me" (Rom. 16:7). So much about Epaphras. As for the fellow workers of the Gospel and of his chains, when he wrote the letter to Philemon he names Mark, whom I take to be the author of the Gospel; and Aristarchus, whom we mentioned above; and Demas, of whom he complains in another place: "Demas has deserted me, loving the present world, and has gone to Thessalonica"; and Luke the physician, who, leaving to the Churches the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles, just as the apostles from fishers of fish were made fishers of men (Matt. 4), so was turned from a physician of bodies into a physician of souls. Of him he says in another place: "I have sent with him the brother whose praise is in the Gospel throughout all the Churches" (2 Cor. 8:18). As often as his book is read in the Churches, so often his medicine does not cease.
passages.notes: The stray "a" before "eadem" is a footnote mark. "Julia" follows the text (Rom. 16:7 usually reads Junia). The opening 'this' refers to Epaphras' captivity discussed just before.
